usage_notes.narrative: Benson instructs that existing Cmaj7 and Fmaj7 arpeggio lines can be directly recycled as D Dorian vocabulary: 'by combining Cmaj7 lines with Fmaj7 lines, we can build a beautiful D dorian line. So, it means that we already have thousands of dorian lines just adapting the major 7th lines to minor chords' (Chapter 2, p. 145).

In Chapter 3, the Ionian (#5) scale -- the relative major of harmonic minor -- anchors the five-zone fretboard system via the Eb+(maj7) guide chord shape. Benson writes: 'Guide Chords => Harmonic Minor & Ionian (#5) = Cm(maj7) & Ebmaj7(#5)' (Chapter 3, p. 238).

Benson establishes that the Dorian scale is a 'static scale, which means that it does not have any avoid note. Therefore, we can play all the tetrads and triads from the harmonic field over a dorian chord' -- listing all seven diatonic tetrads and triads of the parent key (Chapter 2, p. 144).

Benson prescribes adding the major 7th to the Dorian scale as a leading tone: 'we can add the major 7th to the dorian scale, in order to make it more melodic. The reason we can do this, is because the major 7th works as a leading tone to the root of the scale, thus creating the illusion of a dominant 7th chord leading to a minor chord' (Chapter 2, p. 144).

Benson distinguishes two tiers: 'We can use dorian ideas over any minor chord as a possibility of color. However, when we have minor chords that do not belong to the harmonic field, there is no other option than using dorian ideas, otherwise the melody will sound wrong' (Chapter 2, p. 144). Dorian is optional over diatonic minor chords but mandatory over non-diatonic ones.

Benson generalizes: 'all the melodic lines in this chapter can be used over any chord derived from C major scale: Dm7 (Dorian), Em7 or Esus(b9) (Phrygian), Fmaj7 (Lydian), G7 (Mixolydian), Am7 (Aeolian), Bm7b5 (Locrian)' (Chapter 2, p. 180).

Benson states that when playing Dorian ideas over a standalone G7, 'we must be careful with the avoid note C, because it can make your melody sound weird or even incorrect... we definitely can use D dorian ideas over G7, but without forgetting to emphasize the B note instead the C note' (Chapter 2, p. 144).

Benson provides a concrete editing rule: 'it is very important to remember that all the lines ending on the C note have to be modified when played over G7 because the C note is an avoid note for that chord' (Chapter 2, p. 146).

Benson frames the harmonic minor scale as reserved specifically for dominant-function contexts: 'we will use its melodies over harmonic situations where we have tension & resolution' (Chapter 3, p. 235). He lists six valid cadential contexts including bare G7 | Cm7, Fm7 G7 | Cm7, and Dm7b5 G7 | Cm7.

Benson warns against landing on the tonic root when superimposing the harmonic minor chord family over G7: 'be careful when using the root of the Cm(maj7), because it can sound weird, making the whole line sound incorrect. So the best thing to do is to forget the root for now' (Chapter 3, p. 308).

Benson instructs that the VII diminished of C harmonic minor (B dim) and its three enharmonic equivalents (D dim, F dim, Ab dim) are all valid superimpositions over G7, because 'all of them are what we call fake diminished chords, because they are G7(b9) [V7] without the root note' (Chapter 3, p. 246).

Benson explicitly prohibits consecutive use of augmented shapes over a dominant: 'Remember that these augmented chords are not to be played consecutively, they are just small melodic cells to help us build melodies using the harmonic minor scale' (Chapter 3, p. 284).

Benson supplies a degree-by-degree substitution table: 'Second degree = Dm7b5: can be replaced by D dim; Fourth degree = Fm7: can be replaced by F dim or Fm7b5; Fifth degree = G7: can be replaced by G+7; Sixth degree = Abmaj7: can be replaced by Abm(maj7) or Ab dim(maj7)' (Chapter 3, p. 335).

Benson establishes that 'B dim will provide us three more equal chords: D dim, F dim and Ab dim. However, all of them are what we call fake diminished chords, because they are G7(b9) [V7] without the root note' (Chapter 3, p. 246). The accompanying table maps each note to its G7(b9) function.

Benson prescribes ascending-only chromatic approach notes when building the chromatic illusion over diminished arpeggios: 'Most often we will only use simple ascending chromatic approaches over the diminished arpeggios. Descending chromatic approaches work differently and we will cover them next' (Chapter 3, p. 260).

Benson rejects a rigid rule for which diminished fingering shape to choose: 'there is no rule about what shape is the best, because it will depend on what comes next in terms of melody. Therefore, the best thing to do is to memorize many single line ideas using the diminished chord' (Chapter 3, p. 248).

Benson carves out an explicit exception to the avoid-note rule for the 4th over a dominant: 'The only exception is when the chord is a Gsus, so the C note will work with this chord as a starting note or even an ending note' (Chapter 2, p. 144).

Benson anchors the entire five-zone harmonic minor fretboard system to two guide chord shapes, the first of which is Cm(maj7): 'Guide Chords => Harmonic Minor & Ionian (#5) = Cm(maj7) & Ebmaj7(#5). 1st Zone: Cm(maj7), 2nd Zone: Eb+(maj7), 3rd Zone: Cm(maj7)...' (Chapter 3, p. 238).

Benson establishes that the ending note must always fit the tonic chord: 'always pay attention to the resolution note because we must always respect the ending chord, which in this case is Cm7, a non C harmonic minor scale chord. Actually, most of the time, the ending chord of a cadence V7/I will not be derived from the harmonic minor scale' (Chapter 3, p. 235).

Benson explicitly prohibits applying harmonic minor lines to the IIm7 chord in a full major cadence: 'when we have a complete C major cadence such as Dm7 / G7 / Cmaj7, we cannot use C harmonic minor ideas over the Dm7, it would not work' (Chapter 3, p. 236).

Benson forbids the natural 6th (A natural in C minor) in any line played over a V7-Im cadence: 'If we have the cadence G7, Cm7, we cannot use the A note (major 6th) to build single lines, because this note is derived from the dorian scale and cannot be played over any cadence' (Chapter 3, p. 261).

Benson mandates a specific technique for descending augmented arpeggios: 'the descending augmented chord shapes will be played horizontally, and for this reason we will have only one shape possibility per string... the George Benson picking technique works much better when we play horizontal ideas' (Chapter 3, p. 284).

Benson maps the three augmented rotations derivable from C harmonic minor to their G7 functions: 'G+: G, B, D# -- (Root, major 3rd, augmented 5th of G); B+: B, D#, G -- (major 3rd, augmented 5th, Root of G); D#+: Eb, G, B -- (minor 6th, Root, major 3rd of G)' (Chapter 3, p. 281).

Benson instructs that all four enharmonic diminished spellings over G7b9 are interchangeable because 'B dim will provide us three more equal chords: D dim, F dim and Ab dim. However, all of them are what we call fake diminished chords, because they are G7(b9) [V7] without the root note' (Chapter 3, p. 246).

Benson restricts chromatic approach direction when decorating diminished arpeggios: 'Most often we will only use simple ascending chromatic approaches over the diminished arpeggios. Descending chromatic approaches work differently and we will cover them next' (Chapter 3, p. 260).

Benson designates Dm7b5 (along with Fm7 and Abmaj7) as passing material only during the G7-Cm7 cadence because it contains the tonic C note: 'We can use the triads and tetrads that contain the C note (Dm7b5, Fm7, Abmaj7) only as passing chords in a melody going from G7 leading to Cm7' (Chapter 3, p. 308).

Benson allows replacing the Dm7b5 (second degree of C harmonic minor) with D dim when superimposing over G7, explicitly to avoid the problematic tonic C note: 'Second degree = Dm7b5: can be replaced by D dim' (Chapter 3, p. 335).

Benson states the anti-scalar principle: 'we use scales only to guide us through the guitar fretboard. When building melodic ideas, we should always mix scales, superimposed arpeggios and chromatic tones, otherwise the improvisation will sound predictable' (Chapter 2, p. 147).
Benson issues a quality-control warning: 'chromatics must be studied very carefully because the borderline between building a beautiful melody or a non-musical melody is very thin' (Chapter 1, p. 5).

Benson specifies how to derive harmonic minor arpeggios from familiar shapes: 'we will use the same scale arpeggios we learned for major 7th and minor 7th chords, but in the major scale arpeggio we will replace the perfect 5th with the #5th, and in the minor scale arpeggio we will replace the minor 7th with the major 7th' (Chapter 3, p. 243).

Benson permits adding the b7 (minor 7th) to harmonic minor lines even though it is not a scale degree: 'we can also use the minor 7th, which is a note that is not derived from this scale but sounds great. The reason we can use both 7ths is because the harmonic minor came from the aeolian scale and both have the same harmonic function' (Chapter 3, p. 235).

Benson's foundational rule: 'we can only use chord tones or chord tension notes as target tones, but not avoid notes. The only exception would be when the avoid note becomes part of the chord' (Chapter 1, p. 1). This constrains what may function as a structural melodic note over any chord quality.
